Both visible hands degraded: gripping hand lost thumb opposition and digit separation; open hand lost digit grouping and wrist transition.
Pose read as energetic through camera and effects while the body itself stayed conservative.

Meso-scale ridges, plane changes and erosion structure thinned before atmosphere and surface finish.
Colour families flattened relative to the value structure.

notes: Kept as evidence about the tool boundary, not about pencil work. The requested local tightening was never exercised, so this run says nothing about the capability it appears to test. Attribution: tool/interface.
observations: The accepted predecessor was not reachable by the image tool as an edit source.

task: Tighten focal line hierarchy on an accepted finished-pencil artifact without redesign

notes: The whole-body acrobatic pose was judged successful, so the failure is localized rather than evidence against action-pose capability. User technical teaching clarified that a normal human/person render should structurally account for four fingers and one thumb per hand before finish; occlusion may hide a digit but must not terminate its construction. The user also distinguished anatomical completeness from functional hand semantics: a grasp-like hand must have a mechanically coherent thumb/finger/contact configuration. No corrective rerender, isolation test, retention test, or transfer test has yet been performed.
observations: The extreme acrobatic pose, foreshortening, silhouette, and overall action read successfully.

The prominent front/right hand failed digit integrity: the little finger began to render, became occluded by the ring finger, and then visually terminated instead of remaining structurally accounted for.

The rear/left hand lacked a clearly resolved thumb, contained incompletely rendered fingers, and suggested a grasp-like action whose spread digits did not describe a coherent grip or contact relationship.
Both visible hands therefore failed independently even though the global figure action succeeded.
task: Produce a finished direct-render image of an original female superhero in an extremely dynamic and acrobatic action pose

notes: The user requested three separate images of ten hands each; the produced artifact was one composite sheet with three rows of ten. That delivery-format miss does not invalidate the sheet as an isolation test of hand execution. User review ultimately scored 22 of 30 hands acceptable after a second-pass correction. A supplied human hand photograph clarified only the broader need to validate whole-hand mechanical attainability; it is not evidence that one exact finger arrangement should be canonized as universally impossible. No retention or transfer retest has yet been performed.
observations: Twenty-two of thirty isolated varied-action hands were accepted; eight contained identifiable anatomical, biomechanical, or rendering defects.

Top-row #4 had incomplete or ambiguous digit count and thumb identity; middle-row #7 read as three long fingers plus two thumb-like branches, showing that five protrusions alone do not satisfy normal hand anatomy.
Top-row #7 began an index-finger chain that then visually terminated or fused into the palm instead of remaining structurally continuous.
Middle-row #8 and bottom-row #4 failed at the whole-hand configuration level: the individual digit forms did not combine into a convincing mechanically attainable hand pose.
Bottom-row #2 had a displaced or dislocated-looking thumb root/orientation.
Bottom-row #3 used a shadow/value mark that created a false apparent bend in an otherwise simple raised finger.
Bottom-row #8 omitted a useful thumbnail/orientation landmark, leaving an otherwise good thumb under-resolved at finish.
The remaining twenty-two hands demonstrated acceptable pointing, open-hand, fist, grip, support, object-contact, and gestural solutions in the same isolation run.
task: Generate thirty isolated human hands across varied positions and actions, including pointing, grabbing, grasping, holding, and related gestures, as a hand-practice drill

notes: This event records the corrected grip sheet after the user rejected an earlier same-view grip sheet and required varied front, side, three-quarter, and foreshortened viewpoints. The user judged 26 of 30 studies passable. Three were definite failures and one additional secondary hand was under-resolved but not counted as a definite failure. Because rigid objects constrain palm orientation and finger wrap, this run suggests object geometry can scaffold hand construction, but it did not eliminate digit-count errors. The run occurred after the first hand-canon intervention; memory consultation remains unproven.
observations: Twenty-six of thirty varied-angle grip studies were judged passable across guns, blades, poles, tools, and other rigid or semi-rigid objects.
Middle-row #14 substituted an object/handlebar-like form where the hand instance should have been, a task-instance presence failure rather than an anatomical hand failure.
Middle-row #16 contained a secondary/bottom gripping hand with only three long fingers resolved.
Middle-row #18 contained one thumb plus five long fingers, a clear extra-digit topology failure.
#21 had a good front hand but an under-resolved string-pulling secondary hand; the user withheld a strong critique because that hand was not fully rendered.
The broad success across multiple viewpoints indicates that front, side, three-quarter, and foreshortened grip views did not by themselves cause widespread anatomical collapse.
task: Generate thirty isolated human hand grip studies across varied viewpoints and foreshortening, using weapons, tools, handles, and similar objects as grip constraints

notes: The user requested a second no-object isolation test with random hand actions, varied angles, and foreshortening. User review identified seven failures and judged 23 of 30 passable. Follow-up technical teaching proposed a preventative construction route: establish the expected character-specific hand topology first, map the digit roots, fully construct the most obscured required digit before progressively nearer digits, count completed chains against the expected topology, and reject hidden construction only after overlap is solved. The user also cautioned against universalizing the human 4+1 topology: established character/species anatomy and references must override the provisional humanlike fallback. This teaching informed a reviewed canon refinement after the event; it is not evidence that the refinement has transferred yet.
observations: Twenty-three of thirty no-object hand studies were judged passable across varied front, side, three-quarter, folded, open, pointing, fist, and foreshortened views.

#1 folded the ring and little fingers unnaturally into the palm; the ring-finger attachment became separated and the buried distal/nail structure disappeared, although the little-finger bend itself was comparatively plausible.

#4 contained a hidden true thumb behind a thumb-like digit that should have been a finger, an unattached middle-finger structure, and additional downstream fingers; the finished silhouette concealed a broken root topology.

#5 had an index finger curled toward the palm without a convincing finger-side palm-wedge attachment near the middle finger, while the thumb sat too far forward and did not attach coherently to the thenar mass.
#12 contained an extra digit concealed by overlap/shadow: a low curled form plus another fingertip emerging behind the index/middle group.
#24 contained five long fingers plus one thumb, a six-digit hand.
#29 treated the thumb too much like another long finger, with weak root/opposition identity.
#30 failed closed-fist mechanics: the curled fingers did not form a convincing coupled closure and the thumb followed an implausible downward/outward path rather than participating coherently.
The error pattern concentrated on digit topology/root attachment, extra digit chains, and thumb identity rather than on viewpoint variety itself.
task: Generate thirty isolated human hands with no held objects, across varied actions, viewing angles, and foreshortening

notes: This was the first no-object isolation retest after the topology-first/root-map/deepest-to-nearest canon refinement. The user explicitly described the 28/30 score as a first-glance assessment and had not completed a later detailed second pass before the training thread moved on, so the score is retained as provisional first-pass evidence rather than a fully adjudicated benchmark.
observations: On first-pass user review, twenty-eight of thirty hands were judged acceptable; only #15 and #24 were identified as failures at that pass.
The sheet no longer showed the earlier broad frequency of obvious extra chains, duplicate-thumb structures, detached roots, or fingers materializing from unrelated palm regions.
task: Generate thirty ordinary human hands with no held objects after the topology-first hand intervention, across varied gestures, viewing angles, and foreshortening

notes: Same-chat post-intervention generalization from isolated hands to hand-plus-forearm continuity. The human demonstrations support a general strain/natural-range observation; they do not canonize one exact pose as universally impossible. No additional hand canon was changed from this event before the later fresh-chat tests.
observations: Fourteen of fifteen hand-and-forearm studies were judged acceptable by the user; #10 was the only hand called unnatural.
The failed #10 did not primarily lose topology; it overpushed an extreme open spread beyond natural-looking human coordination.

User-supplied hand photographs demonstrated that even at maximal voluntary spread the long fingers retain slight natural flexion and asymmetric tension, with strain propagating into the wrist and forearm.
task: Generate fifteen ordinary human hands attached to forearms with extreme foreshortening and pushed axes while remaining within human mechanical norms

notes: This is the key fresh-chat retention event for the topology intervention. It supports persistence of the improved behavior across conversation boundaries without proving which package component caused the improvement. The residual #5 miss shows the procedure is materially better but still stochastic.
observations: Fourteen of fifteen hands were topology-valid on review, a 93.3 percent fresh-chat result.
#5 was the single hard topology failure: one thumb and only three convincing long-finger chains, with no plausible occlusion accounting for the missing fourth long finger.

#13 retained viable digit topology but value/shading around the raised middle finger created a false articulation or segmentation cue; it was classified as rendering-induced anatomical ambiguity rather than topology failure.
The fresh chat received no renewed topology-first, root-map, deepest-to-nearest, thumb-separation, or prior-failure coaching before generation.
task: In a fresh chat with the unchanged topology archive and no renewed hand teaching, generate fifteen random ordinary human hands attached to forearms using extreme foreshortening while staying within human mechanics

notes: Warm production-transfer evidence only: this image was made in the same fresh conversation after the 15-hand benchmark had already received hand-specific feedback. It is useful integration evidence but is not the clean cold-transfer benchmark.
observations: Both materially visible hands were judged good by the user under full-character production load.
The large foreground open hand preserved human digit topology under aggressive foreshortening, and the rear staff hand read as a coherent grip.
The image simultaneously carried full-body twist, costume, perspective, environment, lighting, and rendering complexity without making the pose timid to protect the hands.
The left foot failed, but that is a separate endpoint/extremity defect and does not invalidate this event as a test of the visible hands.
task: Produce a demanding full-body acrobatic superhero image in the same fresh chat after the hand-retention benchmark, with one large foreshortened open hand and a second hand gripping a staff

notes: Cold fresh-chat full-production evidence. Topology transfer passed, while object-contact/function transfer remained partial because one firearm grip was mechanically wrong. This supports keeping topology and function/contact/load as separate gates and does not justify another topology-canon change.
observations: The both-open-hands render provided clean cold full-production topology transfer: the large foreground hand and the distant open rear hand retained coherent human topology, root continuity, and hand-to-forearm attachment under strong action, foreshortening, costume, environment, lighting, and perspective load.

In the handgun render, the foreground hand topology also held and the rear weapon hand was broadly anatomically coherent, but the hand did not seat around and control the pistol grip in a mechanically convincing way for the depicted action.
The firearm defect was classified as function/contact/load failure rather than digit-topology failure: anatomy can be present while object interaction remains wrong.
Whole-body action remained strong in both outputs, so the hand improvement did not require retreating to a safe or static figure pose.
task: In a new clean chat with the unchanged topology archive and no hand-specific teaching, produce two full-body dynamic female action renders: one with both hands open and one with a rear hand holding a handgun

notes: Fresh-chat cold baseline. Exact canonical Stage 3 predecessor was supplied directly to the native image tool. No user teaching about Finished Pencils was provided before generation.
observations: The cold Stage 4 result advanced beyond Stage 3 through darker values, denser hatching, more surface activity, and some cleanup, but still read as a tightened developed-pencil image rather than terminal Finished Pencils.

Important contours and boundaries remained multi-stroked or search-bearing, too much provisional Stage 3 mark inventory survived, and subordinate regions remained broadly busy rather than intentionally organized.

The failure reproduced the earlier under-resolution pattern without exposure to prior failed Stage 4 images or advance diagnosis, supporting a Stage 4 threshold/calibration issue rather than one isolated stochastic miss.
task: In a fresh chat with the pre-Stage4 source archive and no prior Stage 4 coaching, complete the canonical Broken Gate Stage 3 drawing as Drawing Stage 4 Finished Pencils

notes: Warm same-chat correction evidence only. This event proves the teaching can materially change execution in-session; it does not prove that a revised source retains the behavior in a fresh chat.
observations: After teaching that Finished Pencils is a resolved Drawing state rather than a fixed look or rendering density, the warm retry materially improved over the cold failure.

The retry shifted from generalized graphite accumulation toward cleaner contour commitment, reduced provisional residue, clearer object boundaries, stronger separation of information classes, and more intentional white-paper and mark use.

The improvement followed teaching to preserve approved Stage 3 decisions rather than provisional Stage 3 marks, while keeping comic, tonal, and hyper-realistic pencil languages all valid when intentionally resolved.
The result was judged an incredible improvement over the failures, but fresh-chat retention of the learned distinction remains untested.
task: Retry the canonical Broken Gate Stage 4 task in the same chat after direct human teaching on Finished-Pencils decision resolution across comic, tonal, and hyper-realistic pencil examples

notes: Warm/context-exposed revised-source comparison. The generating chat had already participated in the Stage 4 teaching and correction loop, so this event is positive quality evidence but not cold retention proof.
observations: The revised source produced a strong Finished-Pencils result whose lead face, contours, spear handling, architecture, and cross-medium Drawing readability were independently accepted by Dev and Audit.
The artifact resolved Drawing rather than merely increasing graphite activity and became the stronger current Stage 4 quality example.
Because the chat was context-exposed, this run cannot establish fresh-chat retention by itself.
task: Using the revised Stage 4 source in a context-exposed chat, complete the canonical Broken Gate Stage 3 drawing as Finished Pencils and review Drawing closure

notes: Genuinely clean fresh-chat retention test. The chat did not receive prior failures, successes, warm teaching examples, face critique, medium-neutrality critique, or the corrective phraseology that produced the repair.
observations: The clean chat independently crossed Stage 3 to Finished Pencils under the revised source without reproducing the historical more-graphite-equals-more-finished failure.
Composition, figure action, spear geometry, costume, architecture, hierarchy, and environment remained coherent and resolved enough that another scene-wide Drawing pass was not required.

The clean artifact was somewhat more tonal and its focal face was weaker than the warm quality example, but Dev and Audit independently classified that difference as local quality variance within a successful Stage 4 pass rather than unresolved Drawing.
The clean result preserved enough Drawing semantics for both Paint and Ink successors; Ink required translation of graphite notation but not substantial reconstruction of unresolved Drawing.
task: In a genuinely fresh chat using the revised Stage 4 source and canonical Broken Gate Stage 3 predecessor, complete Drawing Stage 4 with no renewed Finished-Pencils coaching

notes: Opportunistic full-production transfer evidence from a portable Art Skill execution that did not contain the Art Memory tree. This was not a controlled hand benchmark, so skill attribution remains unproven and the event should not erase the earlier firearm-specific function/contact/load failure.
observations: Multiple visible hands retained coherent ordinary-human topology under two-character overlap, foreshortening, wet clothing, tattoos, environment, and full rendering load.
The lower supporting hand under the seated woman's thigh communicated convincing palm seating, digit wrap, contact, and body-load support rather than a decorative or floating hand pose.
The second supporting hand at the woman's torso/waist and the woman's shoulder/neck contact hand remained anatomically coherent and mechanically readable at the working image scale.
No obvious recurrence of the historical extra/missing digit-chain or duplicate-thumb failure class was observed.
Because the deployed Skill lacked the Art Memory files, this result supports that useful hand behavior can transfer from the canonical Skill library itself rather than depending on Memory retrieval.
